items.name: Plain language
items.one_line: Use common words, short sentences and a clear order so the intended reader understands on first read.

sources.title: digital.gov plain language guide
sources.supports: US federal plain language guidance

sources.title: GOV.UK: Use clear language
sources.supports: plain English rules for government content

sources.title: Plain language (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition and history

items.name: Plain-text style email
items.one_line: Write some emails like a personal note (no heavy design, one link, a person's name in the signature) where it suits the relationship.

sources.title: Litmus: A/B testing HTML vs plain text emails
sources.supports: Litmus's own test: results differed by audience (customers vs non-customers)

sources.title: Litmus: Best practices for plain text emails
sources.supports: why and how to write the plain-text version

items.note: One company's test, not a law; test on your own list (edit:ab_test_copy).

items.name: Positive form
items.one_line: Say what is, not what is not ('forgot', not 'did not remember'); avoid double negatives.

sources.title: Strunk, The Elements of Style (1920 ed., public domain, Project Gutenberg)
sources.supports: rule 11: put statements in positive form

sources.title: GOV.UK: Use clear language
sources.supports: negative contractions are often misread as the opposite

items.name: Power words (loaded language)
items.one_line: Choose a few emotionally charged words at decision points; strip the ones that only inflate.

sources.title: Loaded language (Wikipedia; 'Power word' redirects here)
sources.supports: words with strong connotations used to influence an audience

items.note: Lists of 'power words' are marketing folklore; the device itself is loaded language. Overuse slides into hype and AI-style promotional vocabulary.

items.name: Price anchoring
items.one_line: Show a relevant higher reference first (cost of the problem, the premium tier, the alternative) so the price reads against it.

sources.title: Anchoring effect (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: first number seen biases later judgements

items.note: Anchor must be honest (a real list price or a real cost of inaction); fake 'was' prices are a compliance problem.

items.name: Progressive disclosure
items.one_line: Show only what most readers need now; tuck detail behind a link, toggle or later step.

sources.title: NN/g: Progressive Disclosure
sources.supports: defer advanced or rarely used information

items.name: The P.S. line
items.one_line: Use a postscript after the sign-off to restate the offer, deadline or strongest benefit for readers who skip to the end.

sources.title: Postscript (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: what a postscript is

items.name: Punchline at the end of the line
items.one_line: Put the surprising or most important word last in the sentence, where emphasis naturally falls.

sources.title: Paraprosdokian (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: a sentence whose latter part surprises and reframes the first

sources.title: Strunk, The Elements of Style (1920 ed., public domain, Project Gutenberg)
sources.supports: rule 18: place the emphatic words of a sentence at the end

items.name: Read it aloud
items.one_line: Read the draft out loud to catch clumsy rhythm, missing words and sentences too long to say in one breath.

sources.title: UF/IFAS EDIS WC193: News Writing for Television and Radio
sources.supports: reading the story aloud is the most important habit when writing for the ear

items.name: Reason-why ('because')
items.one_line: Give the reader a real reason for every claim and request, joined with 'because'; a stated reason makes compliance more likely.

sources.title: Langer, Blank & Chanowitz (1978), The mindlessness of ostensibly thoughtful action, JPSP 36(6)
sources.supports: copier study: requests with a reason, even a placebic one, got more compliance for small requests

sources.title: Full text of the 1978 copier study (hosted copy)
sources.supports: the effect of a placebic reason disappeared when the request was larger

items.note: The empty-'because' effect only held for a small favour; for bigger asks the reason must be real. Do not cite the study as proof that any 'because' works.

items.name: Reciprocity (give first)
items.one_line: Give genuine value before the ask (a useful tip, template, free sample) so the request lands as a fair exchange.

sources.title: Cialdini: Seven Principles of Persuasion (Influence at Work)
sources.supports: Reciprocity is one of the seven principles

sources.title: Reciprocity (social psychology) (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: background on the norm

items.name: Retention re-hooks
items.one_line: Plant a new reason to keep watching at the points viewers usually drop (a tease, a question, a stakes reminder), not only at the start.

sources.title: YouTube Help: Measure key moments for audience retention
sources.supports: intro, top moments, spikes and dips; intro measures how many still watch after the first 30 seconds

items.name: Rhetorical question
items.one_line: Ask a question the reader answers in their head, to pull them in or make a point land.

sources.title: Rhetorical question (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition of the device

items.note: GOV.UK advises against questions as headings because they are hard to frontload; keep rhetorical questions for body copy and hooks.

items.name: Risk reversal (guarantee)
items.one_line: Move the risk from buyer to seller with a clear, specific guarantee and say exactly how to claim it.

sources.title: Money-back guarantee (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: what a satisfaction guarantee is and why sellers use it

items.name: Rule of three
items.one_line: Group items in threes for rhythm and memorability; the third item carries the weight or the twist.

sources.title: Rule of three (writing) (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: triads are more satisfying and memorable

sources.title: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing
sources.supports: lists overuse of the rule of three as an AI tell

items.note: Reflexive triplets in every sentence are a listed AI tell; use once or twice per piece.

items.name: Structure-friendly formatting
items.one_line: Present steps, specs, prices and Q&A as real headings, lists and tables so machines and skimmers can parse them.

sources.title: Google Search Central: Introduction to structured data
sources.supports: how structured data describes page content

sources.title: Google Search Central: AI features and your website
sources.supports: no special schema.org structured data is needed for AI features

items.name: Search-intent matching
items.one_line: Work out what the searcher wants to do (know, do, go somewhere, visit in person) and give that format first.

sources.title: Google: Search Quality Rater Guidelines, an overview
sources.supports: how raters judge whether results meet the user's need/intent

sources.title: User intent (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: types of search intent

items.name: Sender-name choice
items.one_line: Use a recognisable, consistent from-name (a person at the brand, or the brand) that matches the email's content.

sources.title: Mailchimp: Email sender name best practices
sources.supports: recognisable, consistent, brand-including sender names

items.name: Sensory detail
items.one_line: Add one concrete sight, sound, smell, taste or touch to make a scene real in a few words.

sources.title: Imagery (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: sensory language evokes vivid impressions

items.name: Sentence-length rhythm
items.one_line: Mix short, medium and long sentences so the prose has music; land key points on a short one after longer ones.

sources.title: Aerogramme Studio: Gary Provost on varying sentence length
sources.supports: Provost's demonstration that varied sentence length creates rhythm

sources.title: Gary Provost (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: author of 100 Ways to Improve Your Writing (1985)

sources.title: Hemingway Editor: Readability
sources.supports: save longer sentences for emphasis or variety and rhythm; do not chase conciseness at all costs

items.note: Provost's passage is copyrighted; cite by name, do not paste it.

items.name: Short sentences
items.one_line: Keep most sentences short and split the long ones; one idea per sentence.

sources.title: GOV.UK: Use clear language
sources.supports: quote: 'Try to split up sentences that are over 25 words long.'

items.note: The 25-word split point is GOV.UK's; other houses differ. Pair with tech:sentence_rhythm so short does not become monotonous.

items.name: Show, don't tell
items.one_line: Replace a summary judgement ('she was nervous') with the action, detail or dialogue that lets the reader conclude it.

sources.title: Show, don't tell (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition and origin of the guideline

items.name: Single-CTA email
items.one_line: Give each email one job and one call to action, repeated if needed, instead of several competing links.

sources.title: Call to action (marketing) (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition of a CTA

items.note: Conversion-lift figures quoted online for single-CTA emails were not traced to a primary; leave numbers out.

items.name: Slippery slide
items.one_line: Make every element do one job: the headline gets the first line read, the first line gets the second read, and so on to the CTA.

sources.title: Upgrow: Joe Sugarman's slippery slide

items.name: SME interview
items.one_line: Interview a subject-matter expert with prepared questions to get the specifics, stories and quotes no desk research gives.

sources.title: Subject-matter expert (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: who an SME is
